# Organization of Lukow Descendants in Israel

## What the memorial book records

The [Organization of Lukow Descendants in Israel](/communities/lukow/records/mention_cd446cd051a84599b941e0b0), or in Hebrew **ארגון יוצאי לוקאוו בישראל**, appears in the publication statement of *Sefer Lukow*. The supplied record identifies it as an organization of former residents and descendants of Łuków in Israel that helped issue the volume. The wording preserved in the source scan—“פון ארגו ן יוצא י לוקאו ו בישרא ל”—is a Yiddish/Hebrew-formulaic reference to the organization of Łuków emigrants or descendants in Israel.

The organization should therefore be understood not simply as a genealogical association, but as part of the postwar memorial framework through which survivors and former residents reconstructed the history of their destroyed hometown. The book concerns the [Lukow Jewish community](/communities/lukow/records/mention_87890fe45352fe83680cda98), described in the same passage as the “destroyed community.” This language reflects the central purpose of a Jewish memorial book: to preserve the existence, institutions, customs, political movements, families, and individual lives of a community whose physical continuity had been destroyed during the Holocaust.

The same publication statement also names the [Lukow Landsmanschaft in the United States](/communities/lukow/records/mention_d1e6810775d8b5569418b612). The evidence therefore points to cooperation between two Łuków survivor-descendant circles—one in Israel and one in the United States. The book was published in [Tel Aviv](/communities/lukow/records/mention_5d1cef93c1bb97ea60854f68), a major center of Jewish publishing and survivor activity, in 1968. JewishGen identifies the volume as *Sefer Lukow; gehelikt der khorev gevorener kehile*—“The Book of Łuków; Dedicated to a Destroyed Community”—edited by B. Heller and published in Tel Aviv in 1968. [JewishGen’s Łuków Yizkor Book page](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/lukow.html) ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/lukow.html))

## A landsmanschaft of memory and responsibility

The available evidence does not provide a complete list of the Israeli organization’s officers, its founding date, membership figures, or its precise legal status. It does, however, establish its role in the creation of the memorial volume. That role is historically significant. Landsmanshaftn—associations of people originating from the same Eastern European town—often became the principal institutions through which survivors maintained communal identity after emigration. They organized mutual aid, social gatherings, commemorative ceremonies, cemetery work, and memorial publications.

JewishGen describes Yizkor books as works commonly published by former residents’ organizations as tributes to their former homes and to the people murdered during the Holocaust. Such books preserved local knowledge that was rarely available in conventional historical archives: names of residents, descriptions of synagogues and schools, memories of political organizations, accounts of wartime persecution, and lists of the dead. In that sense, the Organization of Łuków Descendants in Israel was part of a broader Jewish survivor culture that transformed displacement into a form of communal historical work. [JewishGen Yizkor Book Project](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/index.html) ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/index.html))

The collaboration with the American Łuków landsmanschaft is also revealing. Łuków’s survivors and descendants were dispersed across several countries after the Holocaust. The memorial book’s joint publication history suggests that the community was remembered transnationally rather than by one local institution alone. Israel supplied one major center of remembrance; the United States supplied another. Tel Aviv functioned as the place where these efforts were brought together in print.

## The community being commemorated

The organization’s work cannot be separated from the history of the [Lukow Jewish community](/communities/lukow/records/mention_87890fe45352fe83680cda98). Jewish settlement in Łuków is documented or inferred from the late medieval period, and a substantial organized community existed by the sixteenth century. The community developed religious, educational, economic, and political institutions, including synagogues, study houses, a mikveh, a yeshiva, charitable societies, Hasidic prayer groups, and Jewish political organizations. The Virtual Shtetl history of Łuków describes the community as an important regional center whose religious authority extended over numerous surrounding localities. [Virtual Shtetl, “History of the Jewish Community in Łuków”](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/99-history/137635-history-of-community) ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/99-history/137635-history-of-community?utm_source=openai))

By the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, Jews formed a very large proportion of Łuków’s population. The demographic record assembled by Virtual Shtetl gives approximately 4,799 Jews in 1897, 8,058 in 1911, and about 6,000 in 1939, although wartime migration and changing administrative boundaries make exact comparisons difficult. The community was economically diverse: Jewish residents participated in trade, crafts, shoemaking, tailoring, food production, small industry, and professional occupations. [Virtual Shtetl, “Demography”](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/100-demography/21230-demography) ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/100-demography/21230-demography?utm_source=openai))

The memorial book’s translated chapters convey the same breadth of communal life. They describe religious organizations, Agudat Yisrael, the Bund, Zionist youth movements, libraries, newspapers, schools, and Hasidic institutions. One chapter records that *Das Lukower Vort*, a Yiddish weekly, was published in the 1930s, while other passages describe Beit Yaakov education, yeshiva study, and the activities of religious and Zionist youth groups. [JewishGen, translated pages from *Sefer Lukow*](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/luk070.html) ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/luk070.html))

## Why the organization’s work became necessary

The community commemorated by the organization was destroyed under German occupation. A ghetto was established in Łuków in May 1941. It eventually held local Jews as well as deportees and refugees transferred from nearby towns and villages. Conditions included extreme overcrowding, hunger, insufficient sanitation, forced labor, beatings, and arbitrary executions. [Virtual Shtetl, “Ghetto in Łuków”](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/116-sites-of-martyrdom/48334-getto-w-lukowie) ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/116-sites-of-martyrdom/48334-getto-w-lukowie))

The principal deportations began in October 1942. Thousands were forced into transports to Treblinka, while many others were murdered locally. Jews from surrounding communities—including Adamów, Wojcieszków, Stanin, Ulan, Kock, Tuchowicz, and Trzebieszów—were brought into Łuków and subjected to the same process of deportation and murder. The final deportation from the remaining ghetto population took place on May 2, 1943. [Virtual Shtetl, “Ghetto in Łuków”](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/116-sites-of-martyrdom/48334-getto-w-lukowie) ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/116-sites-of-martyrdom/48334-getto-w-lukowie))

Against this background, the phrase “dedicated to a destroyed community” was not merely a literary title. It expressed the historical reality that the living institutions of Jewish Łuków had been annihilated. The descendants’ organization in Israel helped create a durable substitute for the lost communal framework: not a replacement for the town itself, but a forum through which its memory, names, traditions, and historical meaning could survive.

## Historical significance

The Organization of Lukow Descendants in Israel is therefore best understood as a commemorative and diasporic institution whose most clearly documented achievement was its participation in publishing *Sefer Lukow* in 1968. Its significance lies in connecting survivors and descendants to the destroyed [Lukow Jewish community](/communities/lukow/records/mention_87890fe45352fe83680cda98), in cooperation with the [Lukow Landsmanschaft in the United States](/communities/lukow/records/mention_d1e6810775d8b5569418b612), and in bringing their work to publication in [Tel Aviv](/communities/lukow/records/mention_5d1cef93c1bb97ea60854f68).

The available record is too limited to establish the organization’s full institutional history. It does not tell us when it was founded, how many members it had, or whether it maintained a permanent office or successor body. But it does show the organization at a decisive moment: two decades after the Holocaust, when former residents and their descendants were still gathering testimony and preserving the memory of Łuków’s Jews. The volume they helped issue remains evidence not only of a vanished community, but also of the determination of its survivors and descendants to ensure that Łuków would not disappear from Jewish historical memory.
